text: Next, we have another virtual talk, which this time I'm going to
remember to announce the title of.
So this is going to be by Oscar Lindenmeyer, and it's about developing and
implementing relational mineral taxonomy model in Emu for
Museum Victoria's mineral collection.
So I'm Oscar Lindenmeyer. I'm Collection Manager of the
Geosciences collections here at Museums Victoria.
And so the collections I look after include minerals,
gems, rock spores, meteorites, and various kinds
of impactites.
And I'm going to be talking to you today about a project that we undertook over the
last year or so to develop and implement a relational
mineral taxonomy model in Emu, our collection management system,
in order to manage mineral identification data
for our mineral collection.
And so I'm going to run you through
what our previous model looked like, what we set out to do with
developing this new model and why.
Walk through some mineralogy specific considerations
that went into building and designing the new model.
Talk you through how we actually populated a whole lot of new
mineral taxonomy records using the
OpenMindat API,
and then go through some examples of what this actually looks like in
Emu.
So first off, a bit of background on the collections that I look after.
There are over 100,000 specimens across these
four sub-disciplines.
And the largest of these, and by far the most frequently
accessed, is the mineral collection.
We have about 57,000 mineral specimens,
and these represent something like 2,500 distinct
mineral species and include 131 type
mineral specimens,
which is around half of all the type minerals that are lodged in
Australian institutions.
So what did the data structure look like prior to adopting this
new model? Well, something like this diagram here, where
although we had a relational structure for things like multimedia
and sites,
mineral classification and identification information was only stored
locally within each catalog record.
And the eagle-eyed among you might notice that there are some slight
discrepancies in the examples I've given
with the group and class. And so this highlights
one of the problems that we're trying to address.
And what does the structure look like in the new model?
Well, the main difference is that we now have a
taxonomy record for the mineral species vanadinite,
sitting in the taxonomy module. And each of these catalog records is
linking to that shared vanadinite record, which contains a
whole lot of data and metadata about the species vanadinite and
its classification.
And some of this data is being mirrored back into the catalog so
that we can query and view that information where
it's relevant.
So the first consideration I'll talk about when it came to
designing the new model
is mineral classification schemes.
So the fields that we had in a previous model in the
catalog were species, variety, group, and class.
Species and group are essentially analogous to
this new set of fields, species, subgroup, group, and super group.
These are terms adopted and defined by the International
Mineralogical Association in 2009, and wherever
possible, we want to align with the peak body
on mineral classification.
We also have fields for other rank and other value.
And so these are used for handling non-standard classification
records, and also for cases like with the amphibole super
group, where
unusually there is a fourth level of hierarchical classification that's
been defined by the IMA.
I'll talk about series more in the next slide, but we
also have--
previously, we had just one field for class, and nominally
we were using Dana classes, but we weren't really,
partly because the data was quite messy, but also because the Dana
classification
system hasn't been updated since 1997.
And so for anything
post-1997, we'd sort of made it up as we went.
And so what we decided to do going forward was
keep Dana class and Dana code as fields
for legacy reasons, and because that's how the collection is organized
But also alongside those have Stront's Mindat class
and code,
which we use because they capture similar
information and also are being continually updated and are
easy to access and import via the Mindat API.
So the next consideration I'll talk about are solid solution series,
and this is an aspect of mineralogy that we have to contend with when
trying to capture mineral classification data.
A good example of this is the solid solution series
between ferberite, an iron tungstate mineral, and
hubnerite, a manganese tungstate mineral.
And
these have analogous crystal structures and
essentially can vary chemically
completely between
these two end member compositions.
And we have the term wolframite, which is a synonym of that
ferberite, hubnerite series. Anything that sits along that
continuum could be termed a wolframite,
but this is a series name, not a species name, even though historically,
quite often
we have had wolframite put into the species field.
And so what we want to be able to do is efficiently
return
any member of the wolframite series, including the ones that have been
classified as ferberite or hubnerite.
But we want to be able to do this without also including, for example,
some of the other species that are in the wolframite group, so we can't just go to
the next hierarchical classification level and search for the whole
wolframite group.
So
the way we have addressed this
is to have a field that is for series
within mineral taxonomy records,
and one species can be associated with
multiple solid solution series. And so
this is a table, and it can take multiple values.
And so if we were to search for
wolframite
in that field, we would
be able to return both ferberite and hubnerite, which should
have that field filled in as they are part of that series, but also we can
have a record that is only cataloged to the level of a series and doesn't have
the species field filled,
and they will all return when you query on wolframite.
And so there are other examples, like olivine is another very common
one.
So most mineral solid solution series don't have a special name like this,
but often the cases where they do represent lots of historical
cataloging.
And another consideration is that
some species, for example,
mimetic and heterophane
have a solid solution series between them, but sit in
different mineral groups. And so
we need to be able to contend with this, and this is why the
series field sits outside of the main
hierarchical classification.
When it comes to representing chemistry, the main change
is, as with everything else, we're moving these
fields from the catalog to being
within a mineral taxonomy record.
We've also tweaked the names because there was a bit of
historical confusion about
what exactly we meant by formula and elements.
Did we mean
relating to that particular specimen, or did we mean that species in
general?
And so including ideal formula and ideal elements, I think,
clarifies this.
Ideal formula is intended to capture a human-readable
formula
within EMu, and ideal elements is a table which contains
separated elements and can be used for Boolean searching.
One other consideration is that
EMu can't handle subscripts and superscripts, although we were
initially told that it might be able to.
And so you can see here an example of ferrohornblende,
where I've shown you the
formatting that we landed on to still capture
a chemical formula in a human-readable way.
So how do we go about populating a whole lot of mineral
taxonomy records with all these new fields,
and also linking these to the existing catalog records
efficiently?
Well, before we did anything, we made sure to duplicate the
data in the existing fields into our legacy data field, which
is a locked free text field, so that's preserved.
This was before any of the changes in EMu, the new
tab in taxonomy for mineral data had been created.
We began creating these shell records, you can think of them
as, that were taxonomy records that just contained
an IRN in EMu,
a Mindat ID, and a human-readable name.
And using those human-readable mineral names,
we went through and systematically linked
catalog records to these shell taxonomy records.
And so all of this was done before the changes to EMu
were actually implemented. And so we were, I guess,
ready to strike once they were
and populate all of these
mineral taxonomy records once the fields were available.
To actually get the data to populate these fields,
used the open Mindat API
Because we had the Mindat ID as a common unique
identifier, it was relatively easy to extract the relevant
data and map it to
our new mineral taxonomy fields.
And there were about 150 non-standard records for
cases like incomplete classification or legacy
data that had to be created manually, but everything else was able to be done
quite efficiently pulling data from the Mindat API.
So this is what a mineral taxonomy record
looks like in EMu. This is
a tab that was added onto the existing taxonomy module.
So this is the same module that's been used for many years to capture
biological taxonomy data.
And because of this, we have access to some of the functionality developed
for that, including things like fields for
publications and linking to the bibliography module.
I won't go too much into the fields that I've already talked about, but some
additional ones that we have here are their IMA status, so
whether a species is valid and what subcategory
of valid is it. Was it
defined by the IMA? Was it grandfathered?
And also the date that that status is applicable from.
So this has been quite helpful in,
for example, we may have specimens that
have been cataloged as now discredited names.
We don't want to just replace that, but we do want to capture that it
is a discredited species.
And eventually, hopefully, that will be
re-identified as a valid species.
I mentioned that initially we used a notes field to
capture Mindat IDs when creating those
mineral taxonomy shell records.
Going forward, we're going to use some existing functionality in the
taxonomy module,
this table called descriptions, and these are sort of generic properties.
They just have a label and a piece of data.
And so we can, for example, capture
Mindat ID,
and also potentially I'll do some experimenting with capturing
other properties of minerals that we don't
need to have dedicated fields for.
I'm yet to see how useful this will be, but I think it could be quite interesting
and relatively efficient to import using the Mindat
API.
Now going back to a catalog record.
This is our mineral tab and all of the grayed-out
fields, so species, series, subgroup, group,
supergroup, Dana class, other rank, other value,
and ideal formula are duplicating from
the mineral taxonomy record for andradite in this case.
One thing you might notice is that variety
is not part of that mineral taxonomy record, and so this is the one
piece of classification information that is still sitting within
each catalog record.
The reason for this is that varieties are quite variable.
There's no real international standards, and
sometimes one
specimen can have
multiple applicable varieties. So it seemed like the catalog was
still the best place to put this.
So to summarize,
I think moving to this relational model for mineral data will
have significant benefits for how we can manage and
interrogate that data.
The ability to link catalog and taxonomy records before
implementing the new fields, as well as
populating most of them quite rapidly
using the open Mindat API once they were available, made the whole
process quite streamlined.
And if anyone is interested in attempting something similar,
especially if you also
use EMu as your collection management system, then I'm very happy to
discuss. So please get in touch
using the email shown there,
and I hope you enjoy the rest of the conference.
